routes.title: Drinfeld modules, t-motives and characteristic-p special values, Part II: multiple zeta values and Thakur's basis
routes.brief: Plan alternating multiple zeta values in positive characteristic and the proof of the Zagier–Hoffman conjectures by Im, Kim, Le, Ngo Dac and Pham. The final theorems are their Theorem A — with s(w) = (q − 1)q^{w−1} for 1 ≤ w < q, s(q) = (q − 1)(q^{q−1} − 1) and s(w) = (q − 1)Σ_{i=1}^{q−1} s(w−i) + s(w−q) for w > q, one has dim_K AZ_w = s(w) for the space spanned by the alternating multiple zeta values ζ_A(ε; s) of weight w, with an explicit Hoffman-like basis — and their Theorem B: for every w the set T_w of ζ_A(s) with s_i ≤ q for i < r and s_r < q is a K-basis of Z_w, so dim_K Z_w = d(w). The roadmap must cover: Thakur's multiple zeta values and Harada's alternating values with their non-vanishing and shuffle relations; Carlitz multiple polylogarithms and their alternating versions with the power sums S_d and 𝔖_d and Carlitz's identity making the two agree on Thakur's index set; the combinatorics of tuples and arrays — the partial order, initial tuples, characters, k-admissibility; the calculus of binary and fixed relations with the operators 𝓑* and 𝓒, the decomposition of an ACMPL into three types, and the resulting weak Brown theorem with the generating set AT_w; the Hoffman-like set AS_w indexed by tuples with q ∤ s_i, its cardinality s(w), and the strong Brown theorem that it generates AL_w; the dual t-motive package — effective dual t-motives, the series 𝔏(s; Q) realising these values as periods, the equivalence of K- and K̄-linear independence, and the improved linear-independence criterion; the transcendental theorem determining all K-linear relations between ACMPLs, with the character-splitting lemma and the Kuan–Lin degree bound; and finally the bridge AZ_w = AL_w and the deduction of both main theorems, together with the record of what the direct AMZV approach gives in small weights. Import, and do not re-plan: the Carlitz module and its period from Drinfeld modules, t-motives and characteristic-p special values (DrinfeldModulesAndTModules), stages DM.0 and DM.2; Anderson t-modules and effective t-motives from DM.4; Carlitz zeta values from DM.6; and the Frobenius-difference machinery with the ABP criterion from DM.8, to which this paper is also routed as a source. Import global function fields and their constants from FunctionFieldArithmetic FA.0. The classical analogues — Zagier's and Hoffman's conjectures, Brown's theorem and the Deligne–Goncharov–Terasoma bounds, including the alternating case — are planned at PeriodsAndSpecialValues PS.9 and should be cited, not re-planned. This roadmap must be designed together with the extraction of Chang, Chen and Mishiba, 'On Thakur's basis conjecture for multiple zeta values in positive characteristic' (PAPER-CHANG-CHEN-MISHIBA-23), which proves Theorem B independently and simultaneously by a parallel route: that paper works with an abstract space of indices carrying the harmonic and q-shuffle products and an explicit rewriting operator, this one with alternating Carlitz multiple polylogarithms and the bridge AZ_w = AL_w. The two developments share the ABP criterion, the Frobenius difference systems, the index sets and Carlitz's identity; the design job should plan the shared material once and then both routes, since each proves something the other does not — the alternating dimensions here, the generating set of all linear relations there. Corrections the design must carry: the strong Brown theorem (Theorem 1.11) needs the transition matrix from AT_w to AS_w to be ±1 on the diagonal and 0 elsewhere modulo D_1, which Propositions 1.7 and 1.10 as stated do not give; the design must run Proposition 1.7 at every step with its free character chosen to match the target and track that all coefficients lie in A (E12); the algebra of §1 preserves characters, and Theorem 3.4's final step and its 'in particular' clause need that fact, or Proposition 2.3, to pass between K-relations among the Li-values and among the 𝔏𝔦-values (E30, E23); Condition (2.1) imposed on the whole tuple does not make the series of the sub-tuples converge (s = (q−1, q−1), Q = (1, θ^{q+1})), so the matrices Ψ_{s,Q} need the termwise bound, which every application satisfies (E14); the setup of Theorem 2.4 takes Q_i in K̄[t], not in (F_q^×)^{ℓ_i} as printed, since its applications use γ_i ∈ F̄_q and γ_i·H_s (E16); the inclusion S_w ⊂ Z_w in the proof of Proposition 4.10 needs the trivial-character (CMPL) version of Proposition 1.10 with Lemma 1.2, not Theorem 4.9 (E31); and formula (*) in the proof of Proposition 4.11 must be supplemented by the corrected relation for U = ∅ (E33).
routes.reason: The atlas plans the Carlitz module (DM.0), its analytic uniformisation and period (DM.2), Anderson t-modules and effective t-motives (DM.4), Carlitz zeta values (DM.6) and Papanikolas's difference-Galois theory (DM.8), and stops at depth one. Multiple zeta values in characteristic p, their alternating versions, Carlitz multiple polylogarithms, the Brown-type generating theorems and the transcendence results are new layers in that roadmap's direction, hence a Part II. The same Part II, with the same id and title, is proposed by the extraction of Chang–Chen–Mishiba (PAPER-CHANG-CHEN-MISHIBA-23): the two papers prove Thakur's basis conjecture independently and at the same time, they share most of their machinery, and the brief asks for them to be designed together rather than as two roadmaps that would duplicate each other.

DM.8 plans the Tannakian difference-Galois theory of rigid analytically trivial t-motives after Papanikolas, which is built on the Anderson–Brownawell–Papanikolas linear independence criterion; the layer does not state the criterion itself. This paper uses it in the form quoted as its Theorem 2.2, and is a source for it, exactly as PAPER-CHANG-CHEN-MISHIBA-23 is.

review.reason: Checked on the p. 14 image. The ≤ on arrays (p. 8) compares only the character χ(ε) = ε_1⋯ε_n, the weight and the partial sums. So the statement of Proposition 1.3 gives, for ε = ϵ = (1,…,1), only χ(μ'_i) = 1, not μ'_i = (1,…,1). review.reason: Quotation checked on p. 25 (and unchanged in the published proof of Theorem 2.11, pp. 19–20). The display does not follow from the results cited. (a) Proposition 1.10 (and Proposition 1.9, from which it follows) says only that Li(ε′; s′) is some K-linear combination of AT_w-elements. It says nothing about integrality or congruences, and a coefficient D_1·c with c ∈ K need not be ≡ 0 mod D_1. What is needed is the reduction algorithm in the proof of Proposition 1.9, with every coefficient tracked. The proof does not say this. (b) That algorithm, run as written, does not give the congruence. Its base case k = 1 with s_1 > q (p. 22) uses C_{Σ,V}(R_1), so the first q split off carries the character 1. Smallest case: q = 3, (ε; s) = (ε_1, ε_2; 3, 1) with ε_1 ≠ 1, so (ε′; s′) = (ε_1ε_2; 4). The base case gives Li(ε_1ε_2; 4) = −Li(1, ε_1ε_2; 3, 1) − Σ b_i Li(1, ϵ_i; 1, t_i). The ±1 falls on (1, ε_1ε_2; 3, 1), and the coefficient of (ε; s) is ≡ 0 mod D_1. Moreover the q − 1 targets (ε_1, ε′ε_1^{−1}; 3, 1) all get the same row mod D_1, so the matrix is singular mod D_1 and the invertibility argument fails. (c) The step can be filled with the paper's own tools, so Theorem 1.11 is true. Proposition 1.7(1) holds for every ε ∈ F_q^× and for k = 1, and its coefficients are −1 (type 1) or lie in D_1A (types 2 and 3). The base-case coefficients −ε^{−1}D_1 and the b_i of Proposition 1.6 also lie in D_1A. In the finite expansion tree, the coefficient of a leaf is the sum over its paths of the product of the edge coefficients. A path with any type-2 or type-3 edge contributes an element of D_1A. There is exactly one path of type-1 edges only. Choose ε so that it ends at (ε; s): when the m-th q is split off s′_i, take ε = ε_{h_1+⋯+h_{i−1}+m}. That path has n − ℓ steps and ends at (ε; s), which is w-admissible and so never expanded. Hence a_{ε,s} ≡ (−1)^{n−ℓ} and every other a ≡ 0 mod D_1. But the i-th term of 𝔏(s_2;Q_2) = Σ_i (Ω^{q−1}θ^{q+1})^{(i)} has Gauss norm |θ|^{q^i} → ∞. Its constant coefficient alone has absolute value |θ|^{q^i}, so the series does not even converge coefficientwise. Shifting the prefix indices by r−k and filling the tail with r−k−1,…,0 turns (2.1) into (prefix term)^{q^{r−k}}·C → 0 with C > 0. So (2.3), 𝔏(s;Q) ∈ ℰ and Prop. 2.3, whose MZ-property vector is the first column of Ψ and contains only prefix series, are unaffected. (b) The slip is inherited: CPY19 (arXiv:1411.0124 source, Eq. review.reason: The quotation matches the images of pp. 55–56. H_r quantifies over U 'of any depth', and the conclusion ⟨AT^1_w⟩ = AZ_w needs U = ∅. For w ≤ 2q − 2, an element of AT_w ∖ AT^1_w has exactly one entry q, and that entry is not in the last position. When it is in the first position, U = ∅: for example q = 3, w = 4, ζ_A(2, 1; 3, 1) with characters (2, 1) over the tuple (3, 1). Formula (*) is 𝓑*_{ε,U} applied to 𝒞_{λ,W}(R_ϵ) through Lemma 4.4, which needs n ≥ 1. It contains ε_n and u_n + 1, so it is undefined for n = 0. The relation to use is then 𝒞_{λ,W}(R_ϵ) itself, which is binary: its D_1-terms are S_{d+1}-terms. The r = 0 base case has the same issue, but there summing R_ϵ over d suffices. I checked this independently. I evaluated at a generator of F_{3^13} and of F_{5^11}, with d ≤ 6 for q = 3 and d ≤ 4 for q = 5. Every array had depth ≤ d + 1, so no term vanished trivially, and dropping any single term broke the identity. (*) holds for U ≠ ∅ in all 51 cases for q = 3 and all 27 for q = 5, including W with entries equal to q. For U = ∅, the literal reading (drop the u_n + 1 families, keep the D_1-terms at S_d) failed in all 39 and 30 cases. The version with the D_1-terms at S_{d+1} held in every case. Summing it over d gives the claimed ζ_A-relation, because S_0 vanishes on arrays of depth ≥ 2. With this relation the induction goes through: every other term has a non-empty prefix and is covered by H_{r'} with r' < r, or by H_r with a smaller w_1. Case for the defence: the proof is announced as a sketch with details in [25], and the fix is routine. The proposition is not used for Theorems A or B, and its bound also follows from Theorem A. So only the proof is affected. The published Proposition 5.11 replaces (*) by a schematic formula (5.9) with no displayed u_n + 1 terms, but it still does not treat U = ∅ separately.
